claims.claim: Congress is the legislative branch of the U.S. government: Article I, Section 1 vests all legislative powers in a Congress consisting of a Senate and House of Representatives.

Congress is bicameral: the House of Representatives has 435 voting members apportioned among the states by population (at least one per state) serving two-year terms; the Senate has 100 members, two per state, serving six-year terms.
The two-chamber design came from the Great Compromise at the 1787 Constitutional Convention, blending population-based representation (Virginia Plan) and equal state representation (New Jersey Plan).

Article I, Section 8 enumerates Congress's powers: lay and collect taxes, borrow money, coin money, regulate interstate and foreign commerce, declare war, raise and support armies and a navy, and make all laws necessary and proper for carrying those powers into execution.

The Senate shares the appointment power: under Article II, Section 2, the president nominates ambassadors, Supreme Court justices, and other officers 'by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,' and the Senate votes on those nominations.

The classic legislative process runs introduction (only a member of Congress can introduce a bill), committee (hearings and markup; most bills die there), floor (debate and majority vote), conference (a joint committee reconciles differing House and Senate versions), then the president's signature or veto; a two-thirds vote in both chambers overrides a veto.
Bills that raise revenue must originate in the House of Representatives (Article I, Section 7), though the Senate may propose or concur with amendments.

Representation has three practical faces: constituents (the people a member represents and answers to), districts (the geographic units House members represent within states), and casework (constituent service helping people resolve problems with federal agencies and benefits).

conflictingEvidence.issue: The House has 435 members today, but the Constitution itself does not fix that number; it requires apportionment by population with at least one seat per state, and the total has been set by statute since the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929.
positions: The Constitution sets a minimum of one House seat per state and apportionment by population, with no fixed total
The House has 435 voting members today, the long-standing statutory size
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states 435 as the current size of the House (matching OpenStax American Government 3e and house.gov usage) without claiming the Constitution fixes the number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The confirmation power is sometimes described as an Article I power of Congress, but the advice-and-consent clause actually sits in Article II, Section 2.
positions: Confirmation is casually described as a congressional power
The Senate's advice-and-consent role is constitutional text in Article II, Section 2
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the confirmation power to Article II, Section 2 via senate.gov and reserves the Article I list for tax, spend, declare war, and legislate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Declaring war is Congress's power, but the president is commander in chief of the armed forces; popular accounts sometimes merge the two roles.
positions: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power to declare war
Article II, Section 2 makes the president commander in chief
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both roles factually and attributes each to its constitutional clause, with no policy commentary.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft made no verifiable factual claims about Congress; its boilerplate text ('Congress is a foundational concept in Political Science & Government...') was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced machine-generated boilerplate with a source-verified lesson grounded in Article I, OpenStax American Government 3e chapter 11, house.gov, and senate.gov.
Attributed the Senate confirmation power to Article II, Section 2 (advice and consent), not to Article I.

sourceRecords.title: Constitution of the United States, Article I
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A primary source; id and URL reused from the phase-4 source registry (same canonical URL). Article I, Section 1 vests all legislative powers in a Congress of the Senate and House; Section 2 provides House members are chosen every second year by the people; Section 7 requires revenue bills to originate in the House and sets the veto and two-thirds override; Section 8 lists the enumerated powers including taxing, declaring war, and the necessary and proper clause. Direct fetch returns 403; the article text is public domain and the clause summaries were cross-checked against OpenStax 3e ch. 11.

sourceRecords.title: American Government 3e, 11.1 The Institutional Design of Congress
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook (OpenStax, Rice University), read via direct fetch with a browser user-agent. Supports: Congress as a bicameral legislature of House and Senate; the Great Compromise (Connecticut Compromise) blending Virginia Plan population representation with New Jersey Plan equal representation; House 435 members apportioned by population (at least one per state) with two-year terms; Senate two per state, 100 seats, six-year terms; Article I, Section 8 enumerated powers including levy and collect taxes, declare war, raise an army and navy, coin money, borrow money, regulate commerce; the necessary and proper clause. Facts synthesized into original prose; no textbook wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: American Government 3e, 11.2 Congressional Election
sourceRecords.notes: OpenStax American Government 3e, read via direct fetch with a browser user-agent. Supports the definition of constituent casework: constituents reaching out to their congressperson for help solving problems such as applying for and tracking federal benefits or resolving immigration and citizenship challenges. Election mechanics themselves are out of scope (sibling topic: elections); only the casework claim is used.

sourceRecords.title: American Government 3e, 11.3 Congressional Representation
sourceRecords.notes: OpenStax American Government 3e, read via direct fetch with a browser user-agent. Supports: representation as an elected leader looking out for constituents; House members drawn from local districts and senators from whole states; the delegate model (voting as constituents wish) versus the trustee model (voting by judgment). Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: American Government 3e, 11.5 The Legislative Process
sourceRecords.notes: OpenStax American Government 3e, read via direct fetch with a browser user-agent. Supports the classic legislative process: only bills introduced by members of Congress can become law; committee referral, hearings, and markup (committees more often kill legislation than pass it); floor debate and vote; conference committees reconciling differing House and Senate versions; the president's signature or veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers to override; revenue bills originating in the House under Article I, Section 7.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. Senate: Nominations (Powers & Procedures)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A primary source, read live via direct fetch. Quotes Article II, Section 2: the president 'shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the Supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States.' Supports the Senate confirmation power as an Article II role, not an Article I power; also notes the Senate has confirmed Supreme Court nominations and cabinet nominations in its history.

sourceRecords.title: The Legislative Process (The House Explained)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A primary source; id and URL reused from the phase-1 source registry (same canonical URL). Supports the description of how a bill becomes law: a representative sponsors a bill, it is assigned to committee for study, if released it goes on a calendar to be debated, amended, and voted on, must pass both the House (simple majority) and the Senate, and then goes to the president. Corroborates the legislative-steps claims in the lesson.
